summary: OSPF advertises each prefix with a small field of flags, but all OSPFv3 Prefix Options bits are used up and few remain in OSPFv2's Extended Prefix TLV flags. This RFC defines a variable-length flags extension for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 so that new prefix properties can be advertised.

plainLanguage.summary: A form's checkbox list ran out of boxes. This adds a longer, stretchy list so routers can say more about each network address.

questions: what to do when ospfv3 prefix options bits run out
what is the ospf prefix extended flags sub-tlv
what is the ospfv3 prefix options field
how many bits does the ospf prefix extended flags field use
subtitle: A stretchable flags field so OSPF can keep describing new prefix properties after the old 8-bit fields ran out.

tldr.problem: Each OSPF prefix carries an 8-bit field of properties, but all OSPFv3 Prefix Options bits are assigned and only 5 bits remain unassigned in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Prefix Extended Flags sub-TLV, with Type 11 for OSPFv2 and 37 for OSPFv3, holding a flags field that grows in 4-octet blocks.
tldr.outcome: No flags are defined yet; the RFC only provides the room and the IANA registries, so future documents can add prefix properties without a new mechanism.

today: RFC 9792 is a Proposed Standard from June 2025 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no flags itself, so it only provides the extension point and registries that later documents can use.

sections.title: Running Out of Prefix Flag Bits
sections.content:
OSPF can advertise each prefix with an 8-bit field of properties. In OSPFv3 this is the Prefix Options field from RFC 5340, and in OSPFv2 it is the Flags field of the Extended Prefix TLV from RFC 7684. The RFC calls both the "existing fixed-size prefix flags".

All the OSPFv3 Prefix Options bits are already assigned. At the time of publication, only 5 bits remained unassigned in the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Flags. The RFC solves this by defining a variable-length Prefix Extended Flags sub-TLV that applies to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.
sections.plainLanguage: The little box of switches next to each address had no free switches left, so a bigger box was invented.

sections.title: The Prefix Extended Flags Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The sub-TLV has a 2-octet Type, a 2-octet Length and the variable-length Prefix Extended Flags field. The Type is 11 for OSPFv2 and 37 for OSPFv3. The Length is the size of the flags field in octets and MUST be a multiple of 4. Otherwise the Link State Advertisement (LSA) is malformed and MUST be ignored.

Flags are grouped in 4-octet blocks. Bit 0 is the most significant bit of the first 32-bit block, and numbering continues into later blocks, so the most significant bit of the fifth octet in an 8-octet field is bit 32. This document defines no bits.

Unassigned bits MUST be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. A sender MUST limit the length so that it signals the bits set to 1, and defined flags beyond the transmitted length MUST be treated as 0. The existing fixed-size flags are unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The new list comes in chunks of the same size. Switches you did not send count as off, so you only send as many chunks as you need.

sections.title: Where the Sub-TLV Is Carried
sections.content:
In OSPFv2 it is a sub-TLV of the Extended Prefix TLV defined in RFC 7684. New OSPFv2 flags SHOULD first be taken from unused bits in the existing Flags field, before using the new sub-TLV.

In OSPFv3 it is a sub-TLV of the Inter-Area-Prefix, External-Prefix and Intra-Area-Prefix TLVs from RFC 8362, and of the SRv6 Locator TLV from RFC 9513.

If several instances appear within the same TLV, an implementation MUST use only the first and ignore the rest. Errors SHOULD be logged subject to rate limiting.
sections.plainLanguage: The longer list is attached to the address entries that routers already send, and if it shows up twice only the first copy counts.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The sub-TLV introduces no backward compatibility issues. A router that does not recognize it ignores it under normal TLV processing, as described in Section 2.3.2 of RFC 3630 and Section 6.3 of RFC 8362.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers just skip the part they do not understand, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA allocated Sub-TLV value 11 in the "OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Sub-TLVs" registry and value 37 in the "OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs" registry. It also created an "OSPFv2 Prefix Extended Flags" registry and an "OSPFv3 Prefix Extended Flags" registry.

Bits are allocated by IETF Review under RFC 8126. Each entry records the bit number, a description and a reference. Bits 0-31 start as Unassigned, and IANA will add further blocks of 32 bits when the previous one is used up. A flag may use one bit or several bits to represent a state.
sections.plainLanguage: Official lists were opened to record what each new switch means, starting empty.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extension does not affect the OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 security models. The RFC points to Section 5 of RFC 7684 for OSPFv2 TLV-encoding considerations and Section 7 of RFC 8362 for OSPFv3 security.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding more switches does not change how OSPF keeps itself safe.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the flags field in octets; a multiple of 4.

fields.name: Prefix Extended Flags (Variable)
fields.desc: Flags in 4-octet blocks; the field may be longer.
